correctness.rationale: The exact unsplit propagator is exp(−2at) times an orthogonal rotation. Nilpotency gives the two products of opposite shears, each with damping q=exp(−2ah). Applying the two orders to a generic vector gives the same exact averaged squared-length identity as the scalar Gram calculation. Fresh independent choices make this a conditional identity at every iterate, proving the all-n law and all three mean-square regimes. The fixed undamped products have trace 2−s² and determinant 1; the endpoint s=2 is a double root −1 and q<1 suppresses any Jordan growth. For s>2 the larger modulus is R(s) and Schur stability is precisely qR(s)<1. For x=s²>4 the sign of R²−(1+x²/2) is the sign of the difference of u+u^(−1) at those two strictly larger than one arguments. The difference is x(x³−8x²+4x−16)/(2(x²+2)). The cubic starts negative at x=4, first decreases and then increases strictly to positive values, so there is a unique reversal. For s≤2 the comparison is strict in the opposite direction from large s. The two strict damping witnesses check exactly, including 21√5>41 for the fixed-order instability at s=3. Independent symbolic checks reproduced both polynomial identities and a high-precision crossover x=7.75025958832555765… (last-place difference from the printed decimal only), s=2.78392880446421576….
residual_risks: Statements are at fixed step size, with independent fair complete orders and mean-square stability; not a classification of almost-sure exponents or correlated orders.

value.rationale: A single shear crossover with exact opposing witnesses shows why two isospectral stable fixed integrators need not stay stable under random interleaving and, conversely, why interleaving can stabilize in mean square. It cleanly separates three stability notions even for an exactly decaying underlying ODE.
residual_risks: No conclusions about optimal randomized algorithms or nonlinear accuracy.
